archetype.name: Playoff Team (run game and red-zone defense)
archetype.definition: A genuinely efficient Chiefs team, second in the league in net EPA. It wins on the league's best run game, a quiet pass-protecting line and a defense that gives little underneath and in the red zone, while leaning on a turnover edge that probably won't hold.

report.headline: Second in net EPA, but turnovers and red-zone stops are flattering the defense
report.take:
This is not the Mahomes-carries-everything Chiefs of the late 2010s. The offense is seventh in EPA per play, good rather than dominant. The engine is a line that ranks first in yards per carry (5.4) and run EPA and has allowed only 7 sacks, the fewest in the league. Kenneth Walker III has taken 141 carries and turned them into one of the league's most efficient ground games. Reid still calls a pass-heavy game: the Chiefs pass more than expected at the third-highest rate in the league. The passing EPA sits only 13th, though, so the run game is doing more of the lifting than the play-calling admits. The defense is a rerun of 2023's profile: stingy on early downs, fourth in success rate allowed, fourth in missed tackles, and second in red-zone touchdown rate allowed.

The record is mostly real. Net EPA ranks second, and the point differential backs a winning team. Some of it is helped along, though. The Chiefs lead the league in turnover differential per game, and the defense has held opponents to touchdowns on 26.7% of red-zone trips. Both numbers tend to drift toward average. The point differential implies 3.9 wins, not five, and the two 3-point wins over Indianapolis and Las Vegas could easily have gone the other way. Last season was the mirror image: positive EPA, a 6-11 record and the worst luck in the league. The truth sits closer to this year's efficiency than to either record.

What the numbers hide is a defense with real holes behind its good averages. The pass rush ranks 30th in sacks and 31st in sack rate. Deep passes against it are 21st in EPA, and tight ends have feasted, with TE1s scoring well over their usual output. That held up while corners Mansoor Delane and L'Jarius Sneed played and the takeaways kept coming. Now Sneed is on IR, Delane is out, and the last two games produced one takeaway. The 3-20 loss in Seattle also showed what happens when the run game is shut down (50 rushing yards): the passing game was not good enough on its own to carry the day.

Where it heads depends on whether the ground game reasserts itself and the secondary holds together. The back half of the schedule is brutal: Buffalo, the Rams, Cincinnati, New England and San Francisco, with most of the hard ones on the road. Denver already sits a half-game ahead and has the head-to-head split. This is a playoff team, but one that may have to earn it from a wild-card spot.

strengths.title: League's best run-blocking unit
strengths.body: The Chiefs rank first in yards per carry and run EPA, and fourth in yards before contact, so the line is creating the yardage, not just Walker. That makes it repeatable rather than a product of a few long runs. The last two games against Seattle and Denver were the weakest rushing outputs of the year, so it bears watching against good fronts.

strengths.title: Mahomes is barely getting hit
strengths.body: Seven sacks allowed is the fewest in the league, and the sack rate ranks third. That comes despite a time to throw that ranks only 22nd, so the line is holding up even when Mahomes extends plays. Pass protection this stable usually lasts, and it keeps drive-killing negative plays off the board.

strengths.title: Early-down, tackle-sure defense
strengths.body: The defense ranks fourth in success rate allowed, sixth in rush EPA allowed and fourth in missed tackle rate. It wins with fundamentals rather than pressure, and short passes against it are third-best in EPA. That part of the profile is skill, not luck, and should travel.

concerns.title: Turnover and red-zone luck propping it up
concerns.body: The Chiefs lead the league in turnover differential per game, and opponents score touchdowns on barely a quarter of red-zone trips. Those two things explain why the points allowed (second-fewest) look better than the yardage allowed (14th). Takeaway rates and red-zone stops are among the least stable stats in football, and the takeaways have already dried up over the last two weeks. Expect points allowed to creep up.

concerns.title: No pass rush, thinning secondary
concerns.body: The Chiefs rank 30th in sacks and 31st in sack rate, so quarterbacks get time, and deep passes against them rank 21st in EPA. That was survivable with a full set of corners. With Delane out and Sneed on injured reserve until late November, the coverage has to hold even longer with less talent. This is the flaw most likely to cost them a game against the strong passing offenses coming up.

concerns.title: Special teams giving points away
concerns.body: Special teams rank 28th in EPA per game, a steady leak that quietly offsets some of the offense's efficiency. For a team playing a lot of one-score games, that is where narrow wins turn into narrow losses.

trend.note: A 5-0 start with two 3-point escapes gave way to back-to-back road losses, including a 3-point dud in Seattle. The run game has slipped well below its early-season level in both games, and the takeaways have largely stopped. Mahomes' passing in Denver was strong, so this is a dip rather than a collapse.

nextGame.headline: Home against a 2-6 Jets team that can't cover short passes
nextGame.body:
The Book has the Chiefs as 9.5-point favorites at home, and the matchup explains why. The Jets' defense is built backward from what usually beats Kansas City. It is seventh against the run by EPA but 28th against the pass, and 31st on short throws. That invites the pass-leaning game plan Reid already favors, with Kelce working underneath and Walker catching the ball rather than running into a strong front. On the other side, Geno Smith runs a passing offense ranked 10th in EPA behind a line that ranks 28th in sack rate. The Chiefs' weak pass rush has a rare chance to get home. The Jets have covered two-thirds of their games, so they hang around more than their record suggests.

Availability cuts both ways. Kansas City is without CB Mansoor Delane and has L'Jarius Sneed on injured reserve, leaving the secondary thin against a competent passing game. DT Peter Woods is questionable after leaving the Denver game with a neck injury. Omarr Norman-Lott has been designated to return but is still listed out. The Jets are missing LB David Bailey, an every-down player, along with DE Joseph Ossai, and they put DT T'Vondre Sweat on injured reserve. That makes their good run defense thinner than its numbers. Breece Hall is reported good to go after a quad injury, which gives their 19th-ranked rushing offense a lift.

waysToWin.title: Live in the short passing game
waysToWin.body: The Jets rank 31st in EPA allowed on short passes and 28th against the pass overall. Kelce, Worthy and Walker out of the backfield can move the chains without Mahomes holding the ball. This plays straight into a pass-leaning tendency the Chiefs already have.

waysToWin.title: Finally get home on the quarterback
waysToWin.body: Kansas City's rush has been one of the league's least productive. The Jets' line, though, ranks 28th in sack rate and 25th in pressure allowed. A couple of drive-ending sacks and an early lead would put Geno in obvious passing downs, where the Chiefs' tackling and red-zone defense take over.

waysToWin.title: Wear down a short-handed front
waysToWin.body: The Jets defend the run well on paper, but they are missing Bailey, Ossai and Sweat. Once the passing game builds a lead, the league's best run-blocking line should be able to grind clock against a depleted front.

waysToLose.title: Geno beats depleted corners deep
waysToLose.body: The Chiefs already rank 21st in EPA allowed on deep passes and are now without two of their top corners. With little pass rush, a Jets passing offense ranked 10th in EPA can take shots over the top and flip a game that looks lopsided on paper.

waysToLose.title: Run game stalls, Seattle repeat
waysToLose.body: The Jets' run defense ranks seventh by EPA, and they sack quarterbacks at the eighth-best rate. If Walker is bottled up the way he was in Seattle, the offense becomes a so-so passing attack facing a real pass rush.

waysToLose.title: Self-inflicted wounds keep it close
waysToLose.body: The Chiefs drew 105 penalty yards in Denver, and their special teams rank 28th. The Jets go for it on fourth down every time. Hidden yardage, sloppy penalties and extra possessions are how a 9.5-point underdog ends up within a score late.

nextGame.watch: How the Chiefs' patched-together cornerbacks hold up when Geno Smith takes his deep shots, and whether the pass rush can make those throws hurried.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real enough to keep the Chiefs in the playoff picture all season. The line's run blocking and pass protection, plus the defense's early-down discipline, are the kind of strengths that hold. The turnover edge and the red-zone stinginess are likely to regress. So is a record helped by close wins, which means points allowed should drift up and close games should split more evenly.

The schedule is the bigger headwind. After the Jets come Atlanta and Arizona, two winnable games. Then the Chiefs face a run of Buffalo, the Rams, Cincinnati, New England and San Francisco, mostly against top-10 offenses and largely on the road, with a thin secondary that may not be fully healthy until late November. Denver already holds the division lead and a head-to-head split, so a wild-card path is as likely as a division title. Expect a winning record built on the ground game, with a couple of losses to the elite passing offenses.
swingFactors: Sneed and Delane returning to the secondary
Whether the run game recovers against good fronts
How much the turnover edge regresses

confidence.note: Seven games with a stable QB and a clear efficiency profile, but turnover luck, cornerback injuries and a hard back-half schedule widen the range.
